title: the ashoka grove
hook: before dawn the most powerful king in the world walks into the garden, and Sita answers him through a blade of grass

segments.voice: Yesterday: ashoka, the garden called without sorrow, and Sita in it, your line, a flame veiled in smoke. Did you send a word to someone grieving quietly? Today, a visitor comes to the grove. Day six hundred seventeen.

Hanuman is still hidden in the tree, working out how to approach Sita, when the garden fills with light and noise. The night is ending. Torches. Music. Ravana is coming, surrounded by his queens, walking straight toward the woman Hanuman just found. Hanuman makes himself even smaller in the leaves, holds perfectly still, and watches. And Sita, seeing who it is, pulls her knees up and wraps her arms around herself.
screen: `TORCHES BEFORE DAWN.` → `RAVANA COMES TO THE GROVE.` → `SITA DRAWS IN.`

segments.voice: Ravana speaks first, and Valmiki gives him a long, smooth speech. He praises her beauty. He offers her everything: his kingdom, his wealth, the place of chief queen above all his wives. Forget Rama, he says, a beggar in the forest. You'll never see him again. Then Sita answers. And before she speaks, she does something small. Valmiki says she places a blade of grass between herself and him. In Sanskrit, tṛṇam antarataḥ kṛtvā: putting a blade of grass in between. Then she answers him, with the grass between them. Readers have taken that gesture several ways. That she won't address him directly. That a stranger is worth no more to her than a blade of grass. That even something as thin as grass is a wall he cannot cross. Valmiki doesn't explain it. He just lets her do it. Then her words are firm. Turn your heart to your own wives, she tells him. I belong to Rama the way light belongs to the sun. Give me back to him, and make him your friend, if you want to live. Ravana's answer is a threat. He gives her two months. If she still refuses, he says, she will die. Then he storms off, and the rakshasi guards close in to frighten her into agreeing. And all the while, Hanuman is in the branches, hearing every word. He now knows how Sita answers power: not with force, which she doesn't have, but with a blade of grass and a sentence that does not bend.
screen: `RAVANA OFFERS EVERYTHING.` · `A BLADE OF GRASS BETWEEN THEM.` · `AS LIGHT BELONGS TO THE SUN.` · then, large: `TWO MONTHS.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Imagine a single blade of grass resting on the floor in front of you. Thin, light, nothing much. Let it stand for a boundary you're keeping, or need to keep: something you won't trade, however sweetly it's asked for. Breathe in, and feel the boundary there. Breathe out, and let it be quiet rather than loud. Steady as grass in still air. The bell holds the time.
The ashoka grove. Where Ravana offers Sita his kingdom, and she places a blade of grass between them and refuses him, as surely as light belongs to the sun.
Your line: the ashoka grove. Today, if you need to say no, say it plainly and quietly, without raising your voice. Day six hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: Sita's blade of grass appears in Hindu storytelling and devotional art, and in some recitations of the Sundara Kanda her reply to Ravana is read slowly and with great respect.

myth: Sita answers Ravana with nothing between them
she places a blade of grass between them first.
Sita advises Ravana to return her and befriend Rama
she tells him it's the way to save his life.
Valmiki explains exactly what the blade of grass means
he describes the gesture; readers have explained it in several ways.

fork.setup: you're Sita, alone and guarded. the king who stole you offers to make you his chief queen. what do you do?
options: put a blade of grass between you and refuse him firmly.
pretend to agree, to buy time.
fork.reveal: Sita places a blade of grass between them and tells Ravana she belongs to Rama as light belongs to the sun.

original.note: Sanskrit tṛṇa, a blade of grass: tṛṇam antarataḥ kṛtvā, 'putting a blade of grass between'.

trapdoor: what you thought: Sita in captivity is simply helpless.
what it means: she refuses Ravana with a blade of grass and words that don't bend.
what a scholar hears: commentators have read the gesture tṛṇam antarataḥ kṛtvā as distance, as contempt, or as a boundary he cannot cross; the text itself never says which.
recall: blesses him in her own form

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Sundara Kanda 18–20 (Ravana comes to the grove; his offer)

notes: tṛṇam antarataḥ kṛtvā: confirm verse number (21.3 in the vulgate) and transliteration.
'As light belongs to the sun' paraphrases Sita's line (ananyā rāghaveṇāhaṃ bhāskareṇa prabhā yathā, Sundara 21); confirm and decide whether to quote it.
Two-month deadline and threat of death: the text's threat is graphic (he says she'll be cut up for his meal); the script softens it to 'she will die'. Confirm.
Readings of the blade-of-grass gesture (distance, contempt, boundary) are summarized from the commentary tradition generally; confirm.

Fresh review: the text says Sita puts a blade of grass between them and replies; 'not to his face, but toward that grass' was an interpretation stated as text, now cut (teach and myth); softened the 'many recitations' claim.
